title: I have not heard (Avot 5:7)
hook: seven marks of the wise: don't interrupt, answer in order, and say "I haven't heard" when you haven't
tomorrow: which is better: a short fuse, or a fast cool-down?

segments.voice: Yesterday, made at twilight: tongs, a rainbow, a talking donkey, wonders waiting at the edge. Today, something much smaller and harder: a blank.

Some apps will invent a whole answer, sources and all, rather than leave a blank. People do it too. The nod in class. The oh yeah, totally, about a show you never watched. The confident guess in a meeting, because a blank can look like losing. And once you bluff, you have to keep bluffing. So what do the wise say when they just don't know? Avot has three words for it, and they're on a list of seven.
screen: `THE CONFIDENT GUESS.` → `A BLANK LOOKS LIKE LOSING.` → `WHAT DO THE WISE SAY?`

segments.voice: Avot 5:7 sets two people side by side: the golem and the wise. Golem here isn't a clay monster. It means unformed, a lump not yet shaped. The wise one has seven marks. Doesn't speak first in front of someone wiser. Doesn't cut into a friend's words. Isn't rushed to answer. Asks to the point, and answers to the point. Takes first things first and last things last. Says of what they haven't heard, I have not heard. And admits the truth. The golem does the reverse of each. Notice how ordinary the list is. Nothing about being brilliant. Every mark is about how you hold what you know, and what you don't. And look at the exact phrase. Not I don't know: I have not heard. It names where knowing comes from. Someone taught it to you, or no one has yet. The Talmud says Rabbi Eliezer never said a thing he hadn't heard from his teacher. That's not timid; it's careful with the chain. So, for this week, when a question lands and you're blank: three words, and a door left open. Not heard, yet. Then a question back: tell me. The blank stops being a loss and becomes the start of a lesson.
screen: `THE GOLEM AND THE WISE.` · `SEVEN ORDINARY MARKS.` · `NOT HEARD, YET.` · `THEN: TELL ME.` · then, large: `I HAVE NOT HEARD.`

segments.voice: Think of a moment coming up where someone might ask you something you can't answer: a class, a meeting, a dinner table. See the pull to bluff arrive, and let it pass. Then say the words you'll use instead, quietly, once: I haven't heard that; tell me.
screen: `A QUESTION YOU CAN'T ANSWER.` · `THE PULL TO BLUFF.` · `I HAVEN'T HEARD THAT; TELL ME.`

segments.voice: I have not heard: one of the seven marks of the wise in Avot 5:7. Honest about the chain, and open to more.
Three words to keep handy: I have not heard, then tell me. Until next time.

howItsDone: In traditional Torah study, saying 'I have not heard' or 'I don't know' is part of the give-and-take; students are taught to name who taught them a teaching and to admit what they haven't learned.

notes: Avot 5:7 paraphrased: seven things in a golem and seven in a wise person: does not speak before one greater in wisdom; does not interrupt his fellow; is not hasty to answer; asks according to the subject and answers to the point; speaks of first first and last last; says of what he has not heard 'I have not heard'; acknowledges the truth. Confirm wording ('greater in wisdom or in years' in some versions).
